# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Construction Spending, also referred to as Value of Construction Put in Place (VIP)

About the Survey

Purpose

To provide monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the United States (including 50 states and the District of Columbia). The population of interest includes all private residential construction and improvements, nonresidential construction, and public construction.

Coverage

Construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia).

Legal Authority and Confidentiality

Title 13, United States Code, Sections 131 and 182 authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct this collection and to request your voluntary assistance. By Section 9 of Title 13, United States Code, your report is confidential. It may be seen only by persons sworn to uphold the confidentiality of Census Bureau information, and may be used only for statistical purposes. The law also provides that copies of your report retained in your files are immune from legal process.

Primary Customers and Users

  • The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
  • Other government agencies
  • Construction-related businesses

Products

The key statistics produced for Construction Spending are monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. The survey covers construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia). Data are shown by type of construction as seasonally adjusted annual rates and in unadjusted dollars.

Data on construction spending are available on a monthly and annual basis going back to 1993.

Statistics for construction are available at the U.S. level monthly, and by division, region, and state annually for selected categories. Private manufacturing is availalable monthly at the region and division level.

Construction spending estimates include the cost of labor and materials, architectural and engineering work, overhead, interest and taxes paid during construction, and contractor’s profits.

Construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia).

Value of Construction Put in Place press releases are issued on the first working day of each month, 2 months after the reference month. Data are shown by type of construction in seasonally adjusted annual rate and unadjusted dollars.

Release and Revision Schedule

Preliminary value-in-place (VIP) estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. by private or public sector and type of construction are available in the Construction Spending press release according to the release schedule.

For value-in-place estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done, two months of data are revised along with the release of each month's preliminary estimates. An analysis of the VIP revisions for estimates is updated with the release of each year's preliminary May data. With the release of preliminary May data on the Construction Spending release, seasonally adjusted annual rates for the previous 88 months are also revised to reflect updated seasonal factors. Not seasonally adjusted monthly estimates of total construction spending by owner and type of construction category are also revised to reflect late reports and revised or new estimates from outside data sources.

I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Let me dig deeper into the methodology, the survey's status as a principal economic indicator, and how the data is used.Let me fill in a few remaining gaps — the OMB clearance, API/FRED access, and historical details.I now have a comprehensive picture. ---

# Research Report: Construction Spending (Value of Construction Put in Place, VIP)

**Verification of your stated information: ✅ Confirmed accurate.** The title, description, collecting survey (VIP), and coverage (new structures and improvements, private and public sectors) all match the Census Bureau's official documentation exactly.

---

## 1. Basic Identification

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Official title** | Construction Spending (also "Value of Construction Put in Place," VIP or VPIP) |
| **Report number** | C30 |
| **Publishing agency** | U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce |
| **Primary collecting instrument** | Value of Construction Put in Place Survey (VIP), which is a composite built largely from the Construction Progress Reporting Surveys (CPRS) |
| **OMB control number** | 0607-0153 ("Construction Progress Reporting Surveys"; current clearance expires **August 31, 2028**) |
| **Frequency** | Monthly, with annual totals |
| **Release timing** | First working day of each month, covering the month two months prior (e.g., October 1 release covers August) |
| **Status** | Designated **Principal Federal Economic Indicator (PFEI)** — the highest tier of federal statistics |
| **Homepage** | census.gov/construction/c30/c30index.html |

---

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Title 13, United States Code, Sections 131 and 182** authorize the Census Bureau to conduct this collection.
- **Title 13, Section 9** guarantees respondent confidentiality: responses may be seen only by sworn Census employees, used only for statistical purposes, and copies retained in respondents' files are immune from legal process.
- **The survey is voluntary** — unlike the decennial census or the American Community Survey, response is requested but not mandatory. This matters for data quality: nonresponse bias studies have been conducted (notably a 2018 study of private nonresidential and multifamily response), and OMB's 2019 clearance included a term requiring the Census Bureau to report on response-rate improvement efforts.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. ch. 35):** The collection is cleared through OMB as ICR 0607-0153. Forms C-700 (private nonresidential), C-700(R) (multifamily residential), C-700(SL) (state & local government), and C-700(F) (federal government) collect data from roughly **22,000 project respondents**, generating ~264,000 responses and an estimated **51,333 burden hours annually** (~30 minutes for the first monthly report, ~10 minutes thereafter).
- **PFEI governance:** As a Principal Federal Economic Indicator, the release is governed by OMB's *Statistical Policy Directive on Compilation, Release, and Evaluation of Principal Federal Economic Indicators*, which imposes strict rules on pre-release access, embargoes, and periodic evaluation. The Census Bureau submitted a formal evaluation of the CPRS to OMB in March 2016 and implemented updated variance estimation programs in July 2015.
- **Disclosure avoidance:** Cell suppression (primary plus complementary suppressions, flagged "D") is the primary method. Releases carry Census Disclosure Review Board approval (e.g., CBDRB-FY26-0231).

---

## 3. History

- **1915–1964:** The construction put-in-place series was compiled by the **U.S. Department of Labor**.
- **1964:** The Census Bureau took over collection. Some annual publications still contain the older Labor Department data.
- **1993:** A **major reclassification** of construction type categories was implemented. The old 1964-era classifications continued to be published alongside until 2002, but **data prior to 1993 are not comparable to the current series**. This is why all consistent modern time series begin in January 1993.
- **Consequence of reclassification:** Before 1993 the Bureau published **constant-dollar (inflation-adjusted) estimates**; since the reclassification it has been unable to do so. All current data are in **current dollars** — a crucial caveat for analysts doing long-run or real-terms comparisons (they must deflate the series themselves).
- **Benchmarking history:** Private manufacturing construction estimates are periodically benchmarked to the Census Bureau's Annual Capital Expenditures Survey (ACES); this occurred for data years 1992, 1994, 1998, 2003, 2008, 2012, and 2017, with a carry-forward factor applied between benchmark years. Federal, utilities, and railroad estimates are benchmarked to or derived from outside sources, sometimes with lags of one to two years.
- **Legacy data:** Historical files for 1964–2002 under the old classification system remain linked from the Census construction pages — a key preservation concern (see §8).

---

## 4. Methodology and Data Production

### What "value put in place" means
It measures the value of construction work **installed or erected at the site during a given period**, regardless of when a project started or when contractors were paid. For each project it includes:
1. Cost of materials installed or erected
2. Cost of labor (contractor and force-account) plus a share of equipment rental
3. Contractor's profit
4. Architectural and engineering work
5. Overhead and office costs chargeable to the project
6. Interest and taxes paid during construction (except for state and locally owned projects)

### How the estimates are built (a hybrid, not a single survey)
This is unusual among federal statistics and important for data users to understand. Only about **65% of total monthly construction spending is directly measured by survey**; the remaining **~35% is modeled or compiled from secondary sources**:

- **CPRS (four monthly project-level surveys):** An independent systematic sample of construction projects is drawn each month; once selected, a project stays in sample until completion (average ~12 months). Owners (or designees) report monthly value put in place by mail, online, or phone follow-up. These cover private nonresidential, private multifamily, state & local, and federal projects.
- **Survey of Construction (SOC):** Source of single-family residential estimates.
- **Consumer Expenditure Interview Survey (BLS, collected by Census):** Source of private residential improvement estimates for owner-occupied housing.
- **Secondary/benchmark sources:** Surface Transportation Board (railroad construction), industry trade association statistics (e.g., cable television construction), federal agency data, and ACES benchmarks.

### Coverage and geography
- **Universe:** All private residential (including improvements), private nonresidential, and public construction in the 50 states and DC — both building and non-building (highways, power, sewage, conservation, etc.).
- **Published detail:** U.S.-level monthly; region, division, and state detail **annually** for selected categories; private manufacturing monthly at region/division level.
- **Type categories:** Lodging, office, commercial, health care, educational, religious, public safety, amusement/recreation, transportation, communication, power, highway and street, sewage/waste, water supply, conservation and development, manufacturing — split by private vs. public ownership.

### Seasonal adjustment and revisions (critical for users)
- Data are published both as **seasonally adjusted annual rates (SAAR)** and **not seasonally adjusted (NSA)** dollar values.
- **Every monthly release revises the prior two months.** With each May-data release, seasonally adjusted annual rates for the **previous 88 months (~7+ years)** are revised for updated seasonal factors, and NSA estimates are revised for late reports and updated source data.
- Annual estimates are finalized with the May release of the following year (two-year lag).
- Average absolute revision from preliminary to first revision: ~0.65% total, ~0.75% private, ~0.59% public construction. Statistical significance is reported with margins of error (e.g., "0.9 percent (±1.0)"), with an asterisk convention when change is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

---

## 5. Who Uses It and Why (Public Benefits)

### Government users (the "primary customers")
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA):** The single most important user. VIP feeds the **construction components of gross private domestic investment and government consumption in GDP** — the National Income and Product Accounts. Construction spending is a significant, cyclically sensitive share of GDP (~4–5% currently, ~$2.2 trillion annual rate as of mid-2020s).
- **Federal Reserve Board and U.S. Treasury:** Use the data to nowcast/forecast GDP; these forecasts are presented to the Board of Governors and **directly influence monetary policy**.
- **Other agencies:** Infrastructure planning, economic policy evaluation, and interagency statistical benchmarking.

### Private sector users
- **Construction-related businesses and trade associations:** Estimate demand for building materials; schedule production, distribution, and sales; conduct market analysis and site/investment decisions.
- **Financial markets:** As a PFEI released at a fixed time, it moves markets and is a standard input to economic forecasting models.

### Researchers, journalists, and the public
- Cyclical analysis of the housing and construction sectors; state/local infrastructure monitoring (the public construction series — highways, schools, water — is one of the few monthly national windows into public capital investment); academic macroeconomics.

### The public benefit case
The dataset underpins GDP measurement, monetary policy, and trillion-dollar public and private investment decisions. At roughly $0 direct cost burden to respondents beyond their time (51,333 hours/year across 22,000 respondents), it is a relatively low-burden, high-leverage statistical program.

---

## 6. Access Points and Formats

| Channel | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Census C30 website** | Current release (PDF/XLSX), historical monthly and annual XLSX files back to 1993, methodology, definitions, release schedule |
| **Census "Time Series/Trend Charts" tool** (program code: VIP) | Interactive extraction of the current series |
| **Census API** (census.gov/developers) | Programmatic access |
| **FRED (St. Louis Fed), release ID 229** | ~96 series; headline series **TTLCONS** (total construction, SAAR, monthly, Jan 1993–present); FRED API and mobile app supported |
| **ALFRED** | **Vintage/archival versions** of the series as they existed on specific dates — essential for revision studies and reproducibility |
| **Subnational files** | Annual state/region/division XLSX; monthly subnational private manufacturing |

---

## 7. Caveats and Known Limitations

1. **Current dollars only** — no official inflation-adjusted series since 1993. Users must deflate (commonly with BEA construction price indexes or the Census/BLS price indexes).
2. **Heavy revision pattern** — preliminary estimates are exactly that; the SAAR series is revised for 88 months. Point-in-time analysis requires ALFRED vintages.
3. **Pre-1993 discontinuity** — old-classification data (1964–2002) exist but cannot be spliced cleanly to the modern series.
4. **Voluntary response** — nonresponse is a persistent quality concern, and Census has been required by OMB to document response-rate improvement.
5. **Limited geography** — monthly data are national only; state-level detail is annual and only for selected categories.
6. **Hybrid estimation** — about a third of the total is modeled from secondary sources, some of which arrive one to two years late, forcing later benchmark revisions.

---

## 8. Guidance by Audience

**For preservationists / data librarians:**
- The *current* files on census.gov are continuously overwritten by revisions. Preservation efforts should capture **each monthly vintage** (PDF release + XLSX tables), or rely on/document ALFRED as the de facto vintage archive.
- The **1964–2002 legacy classification files** are a high-risk asset: they live only as legacy links on the Census construction pages and are not part of the actively maintained series.
- Key metadata to preserve alongside the data: methodology PDFs, definitions PDF, Federal Register notices (e.g., 2024 ICR, FR Doc. 2024-15599), OMB ICR packages at reginfo.gov (0607-0153), and DRB approval numbers.
- Suggested citation form (per FRED): *U.S. Census Bureau, Total Construction Spending: Total Construction in the United States [TTLCONS], retrieved from FRED, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.*

**For data scientists:**
- Use the Census API or FRED API for programmatic pulls; prefer NSA values if doing your own seasonal work.
- Never mix pre-1993 and post-1993 series without explicit treatment; deflate explicitly for real-terms analysis; respect the ± margin-of-error convention when reporting month-over-month changes.

**For policy activists:**
- The **public construction series** (highway, educational, water supply, sewage, conservation) is the tool for tracking national infrastructure investment trends; state-level annual tables support subnational advocacy.
- Engagement channels for defending or improving the dataset: Federal Register comment periods on the triennial OMB ICR renewals (next renewal due before the August 2028 expiration), the Census Bureau's advisory committees, and appropriations oversight of the Economic Directorate.

---

## Key Sources
- Census Bureau, Construction Spending: About the Survey, Methodology, Forms, Historical Data — census.gov/construction/c30/
- OMB ICR 0607-0153, Construction Progress Reporting Surveys — reginfo.gov
- Federal Register, Vol. 89 (July 16, 2024), Doc. 2024-15599 (uses and needs statement)
- Census Bureau 2014 VIP webinar transcript (history: DOL 1915–1964, Census 1964+, 1993 reclassification)
- FRED release 229 and series TTLCONS — fred.stlouisfed.org
- Non-response Bias Study for Value of Construction Put in Place (2018 ICR supporting document)

Now let me check release timeliness (including shutdown impacts), the ICR renewal status, and any policy-driven changes to economic surveys.One more round of research on the proposed statistical agency reorganization and leadership status, to complete the Policy and Staffing assessments.# Risk Assessment: Construction Spending (Value of Construction Put in Place, C30/VIP)

**Assessment basis:** Research conducted on the Census Bureau's current operations, FY2026 budget, OMB ICR records, 2025 release history, and administration policy actions. Key institutional context: the publisher (Census Bureau) has experienced substantial disruption in 2025, but this specific dataset — a Principal Federal Economic Indicator feeding GDP — has so far been among the most protected products in the federal statistical system.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- Census C30 pages still host the complete historical archive: monthly and annual XLSX files back to 1993, legacy 1964–2002 files under the old classification system, and a press-release PDF archive with 2025 releases fully posted (census.gov/construction/c30/historical_data.html; prpdf.html).
- Independent mirrors exist and are intact: FRED release 229 (~96 series, TTLCONS back to Jan 1993) and ALFRED vintage data, which archive every revision — providing redundancy even if census.gov files were altered.
- No reports of retroactive file removal or alteration of the construction series in 2025.

**Evidence for higher levels:** None found. (Structural fragility — the legacy 1964–2002 files exist only as legacy links, and revised SAAR values are continuously overwritten — predates this administration and is a preservation concern, not an observed removal.)

**➡️ Selected: No Known Issue.** All prior-cycle data remain accessible with no known alterations; the main archival risk is latent (legacy files, lack of Census-maintained vintages) rather than actualized.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- The October–November 2025 government shutdown (43 days, longest in history) delayed the August 2025 release from Oct 1 to Nov 17, 2025, and disrupted subsequent releases ("Next release: TBD" appeared on the November release; September/October data were combined in a single Nov/Dec release). There was "no collection or processing in October" (Census Bureau PFEI recovery plan, via The Census Project, Dec 2025).
- Census's recovery plan explicitly commits to "no gaps or missing reference periods," and the published release schedule now shows normal future dates through 2027 — so publication was delayed, not skipped.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- ICR 0607-0153 was renewed **before expiration**: OIRA concluded 8/18/2025 (previous expiry 8/31/2025), new expiration 8/31/2028 — active, regular "extension without change" review.
- Releases resumed post-shutdown; all reference periods are being preserved per the recovery plan.

**Evidence for High Risk:** Not met — C30 has no statutory publication deadline (PFEI scheduling is administrative), the ICR never lapsed, and no reference period was skipped.

**➡️ Selected: Moderate Risk.** The rubric's moderate definition — "typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed" — was squarely triggered by the shutdown, though the ICR is active through August 2028 and the series itself shows no gap. Note the underlying vulnerability: because funding lapsed, a PFEI simply stopped publishing; recurring appropriations brinksmanship makes this repeatable.

---

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence for Moderate Risk (potential/emerging risk):**
- Census-wide staffing loss of ~15% since FY24 plus a hiring freeze directly strain survey operations — including the Economic Indicators Division that produces C30 (American Statistical Association, *The Nation's Data at Risk: 2025*; GovExec July 2025).
- Commerce's requirement that the Secretary personally approve contracts over $100,000 created a backlog of 3,000+ requests, potentially delaying survey operations contracts.
- All four external advisory committees — including the Federal Economic Statistics Advisory Committee (FESAC), which provided methodological review of economic indicators — were terminated in March 2025, removing a quality-assurance channel.
- The shutdown forced compressed/condensed processing schedules to catch up, a documented near-term quality stressor.
- Pre-existing weakness: the CPRS is a **voluntary** survey with documented nonresponse-bias concerns (2018 study; OMB terms of clearance on response rates), making it sensitive to reduced follow-up capacity.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- No documented reduction in granularity, frequency, or published detail of the C30 tables; the November 2025 release contains the full standard table set, margins of error, and revision schedule.
- FY2026 request kept Current Economic Statistics flat at $216M; enacted FY2026 bill (P.L. 119-74) funds Current Surveys & Programs at $319M, above the request.

**Evidence for High Risk:** Not met — no actual reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency of the published series have occurred.

**➡️ Selected: Moderate Risk.** The product itself is unchanged, but the production environment (staffing, hiring freeze, contract backlog, loss of advisory review, catch-up processing) constitutes exactly the "potential or emerging risk" the moderate tier describes.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- Authority is explicitly named: Title 13 U.S.C. §§131 and 182 authorize the collection; confidentiality under Title 13 §9.
- The data are required for implementation of a core federal program: BEA uses VIP for the construction components of GDP (NIPAs), and the Federal Reserve and Treasury use it for policy. There is no adequate alternative collection — private sources (e.g., Dodge/ConstructConnect) are not statistical substitutes, and the BEA dependency is structural.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- Title 13 §§131/182 *authorize* current surveys but do not *mandate* a monthly construction put-in-place series specifically (unlike the decennial census or the quinquennial economic census, which §131 explicitly requires). The FY2026 Census budget justification states the Bureau "will have eliminated functions that are not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" — placing non-mandated current surveys in a scrutinized category.

**Evidence for High Risk:** Not met — authorization is not vague, programmatic use (GDP) is explicit and central, and no substitute exists.

**➡️ Selected: Moderate Risk.** This matches the rubric's moderate tier precisely: not explicitly required by statute, but required for implementation of a federal program (GDP/NIPAs, monetary policy) with no alternative data collection. The strong statutory-authority naming and GDP dependency make it the most defensible possible member of that tier — but the administration's "statutorily mandated" filter for program survival is a live structural vulnerability.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for High Risk:**
- **Staff losses >1,000:** AFGE Council 241 reports ~1,300–1,500 Census employees lost since January 2025 (deferred resignations, early retirements) out of ~13,230 (Sept 2024 OPM figure) — a 10–15% decline that exceeds the rubric's 1,000-person absolute threshold for High (AP News, Oct 2025; Bloomberg Law; ASA 2025 report: "lost an estimated 15% in staffing since FY24").
- **Leadership removed:** Director Rob Santos resigned in February 2025 (mid-term); COO Ron Jarmin served extended acting duty; 18 top-leadership vacancies were reported; the ASA reports the acting director role was subsequently filled by a political appointee holding another full-time position. ~100 additional RIF notices were issued to Census call-center staff during the October 2025 shutdown.

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- If measured by percentage only, losses (10–15%) fall in the 10–39% moderate band.
- Budget: FY2026 enacted (P.L. 119-74) provides $1.49B overall (+$108M vs FY2025); Current Surveys & Programs at $319M is only a ~3% cut; the C30-relevant Current Economic Statistics line was flat at $216M in the request — well under the 10% budget-cut threshold.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:** Not met — staffing losses far exceed 10% at the agency level and leadership changed.

**➡️ Selected: High Risk.** Under the rubric's disjunctive criteria, both "1,000 or more staff lost" and "leadership removed" are triggered at the publishing agency. Important caveat for calibration: these figures are agency-wide, and losses are not broken out for the Economic Indicators Division specifically; funding for the economic-statistics accounts that produce C30 has been essentially flat. If the rubric were applied strictly at the division level, Moderate would be arguable — but at the agency level as worded, High is the correct call.

---

## 6. Policy

**Evidence for Moderate Risk:**
- **Proposed reorganization:** The FY2026 President's Budget (May 2025) and the administration's August 2025 workforce plan propose reorganizing/consolidating BLS, BEA, and Census within Commerce — echoing Project 2025's blueprint to merge the statistical agencies and to "review and potentially downsize or eliminate various Census Bureau programs." This is a pending change that would directly affect C30's institutional home.
- **Hostile context toward statistical agencies:** Unsubstantiated claims of biased economic data by administration officials, the firing of the BLS commissioner (Aug 2025), termination of statistical advisory committees, and an executive order altering the constitutional basis of the decennial census (ASA 2025 report).
- The FY2026 budget's directive to eliminate non-statutorily-mandated functions is an administration statement suggesting change is planned, without naming which programs.

**Evidence for No Known Issue:**
- The CPRS ICR renewal was **not** a Presidential Action-driven ICR: it was a routine "extension without change" initiated under the prior administration (Nov 2024), concluded 8/18/2025, with unchanged burden and forms.
- No negative policy notes appear on the C30 web pages; the dataset's content, categories, and release format are unchanged since January 2025. Construction spending data are politically neutral and have not been named in any administration criticism.

**Evidence for High Risk:** Not met — no Presidential-Action ICR, no negative policy note on site, no changes to what is collected or published.

**➡️ Selected: Moderate Risk.** The rubric's moderate tier — "proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned" — fits the reorganization proposal and the non-mandated-functions directive. Nothing yet targets construction statistics specifically, but the dataset sits inside an institution explicitly slated for restructuring.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Level | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | **No Known Issue** | Full archives (1993–present, plus 1964–2002 legacy) intact; FRED/ALFRED mirrors provide redundancy |
| **Future Data Availability** | **Moderate Risk** | Shutdown caused a 6+ week delay and disrupted schedule, but ICR is active through Aug 2028 and no reference period was skipped |
| **Data Quality** | **Moderate Risk** | Series output unchanged, but staffing losses, hiring freeze, contract backlog, and advisory-committee terminations are emerging threats |
| **Statutory Context** | **Moderate Risk** | Explicit Title 13 authorization and irreplaceable GDP role, but the monthly series is not statutorily mandated — a liability given the "eliminate non-mandated functions" directive |
| **Staffing and Funding** | **High Risk** | ~1,300–1,500 staff lost (>1,000 threshold) and director-level leadership removed/acting, though C30-relevant budget lines are roughly flat |
| **Policy** | **Moderate Risk** | Pending BLS/BEA/Census reorganization proposal and hostile rhetoric toward statistical agencies; no direct action against this dataset |

**Overall assessment:** The Construction Spending dataset is among the *lower-risk* federal datasets in the current environment — it is a Principal Federal Economic Indicator with an irreplaceable role in GDP, an active ICR through 2028, intact archives, and no direct political targeting. Its risks are almost entirely *institutional and inherited* from the Census Bureau's situation (staffing losses, leadership instability, reorganization proposals, funding-lapse vulnerability) rather than *dataset-specific*. The single most consequential near-term watch items are: (1) whether the FY2027 budget's reorganization proposal advances in Congress, (2) whether the "non-statutorily mandated functions" elimination reaches current economic surveys, and (3) the stability of CPRS response rates amid reduced survey-operations staffing. Preservationists should treat the legacy 1964–2002 files and monthly release vintages as the highest-priority capture targets, since ALFRED is currently the only systematic vintage archive.
